input: ...the analogy can also be tested against the measurements from the packed bed, where the Reynolds number is 20000. Taking $f$ = 0.0064 from the pressure-drop measurements, the Chilton-Colburn analogy gives $j_D$ = $f$/2 = 0.0032, and this value is found to be in good agreement with the mass transfer measured in the bed, within the usual scatter of such data. Results of this kind are frequently cited in support of the analogy, because they suggest that the same surface processes govern both the friction and the transfer. It is important to recognise, however, that the agreement depends on the pattern of the flow. When the flow is directed across a surface rather than along it, form drag contributes to the pressure drop without contributing anything to the transfer at the surface, and the two quantities that the analogy equates are no longer measuring the same thing. Under those conditions, $f$ reflects both contributions whereas $j_D$ reflects only the transfer, so the analogy will tend to overstate the transfer, and the careful reader will treat values obtained in that geometry with some caution The point is worth emphasising because the failure is not random: it follows from the geometry, and it will appear whenever the flow is arranged in that way, whatever the fluid or the surface material may be....
target: ...where the analogy is applied to a packed bed at a Reynolds number of 20000, the comparison runs as follows. With $f$ = 0.0064 from the pressure-drop measurements, the Chilton-Colburn analogy gives $j_D$ = $f$/2 = 0.0032, and the measured mass transfer agrees with the stated value within the scatter of the bed data. Agreement of that kind is the ground on which the analogy is used for beds of this packing: at the surface, the same exchange sets both the friction and the transfer, and the two factors state it in the same terms. The agreement does not survive a change in the flow pattern. Where the flow meets a surface across its direction, form drag adds a part of the pressure drop that has no counterpart in the transfer at the surface, and the two sides of the analogy separate. In that case $f$ gathers both parts while $j_D$ gathers only the transfer part, and equating them overstates the transfer by the form-drag share. The distinction is one of mechanism: friction at a surface and transfer at the same surface share the near-surface exchange, while form drag arises from the pressure field around the body and has no share in that exchange. That is why the failure is systematic rather than scattered: the analogy does not merely lose accuracy, it assigns to transfer a part of the drop that belongs elsewhere. The analogy is therefore applied where the flow runs along the surface, and a bed or bundle in cross-flow is treated on its own measurements rather than on the analogy's value...
